# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–21 (Complete – Updated 153)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Spring of sixth year** (Chapter 21). Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, and Amelia's maternal sacrifice. **Chapter 20 events**: Sir Pitt (elder) dies summer 1816; Pitt becomes Baronet and MP; Miss Crawley dies spring 1816; house renovation November through winter on Great Gaunt Street; Christmas gathering at Queen's Crawley; return to London with house ready for Pitt's family; Parliament session begins with Pitt establishing himself as profound dissembler.
- **Locations**: Salwick (harbor town); Harrowgate; Dunholt; London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gaunt House; Gulton (river crossing); Lombard Street (bank location); Brussels (referenced from ten years prior); Bryngate (Fedette Orlwood and Madrek Orlwood lodgings).
- **Parliamentary and financial context**: Pitt attends first session assiduously, learns House routine thoroughly, presents petition from Mudbury, makes acquaintance with ministers and party chiefs, determines to rank among them.

## Main Characters

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)**
- **Court presentation achievement (Chapter 21)**: Rebecca's primary ambition realized when she gains presentation at Court through Lady Jane's sponsorship. Covets "certificate of virtue" from Lord Chamberlain. **Presentation dress**: Uses lace and brocade from old wardrobes of Pitt's house—materials she "quietly carried home" while Pitt put house in order. Briggs witnessed but sympathized. Emerges pronounced "charmante."
- **Court jewels scheme (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Court diamonds and pearl necklace hired from Mr. Polonius of Coventry Street. **Pitt's secret gift**: Diamond clasp omitted from Lady Jane's knowledge; Pitt blushed when mentioned. **Steyne's financing**: Diamonds **never returned** to Polonius; hidden in Amelia's old desk given years ago, containing valuables unknown to Rawdon. **Steyne financed the diamonds** and "knew whence the jewels came and who paid for them."
- **Post-presentation virtue performance**: After Court, cuts dubious acquaintances (Lady Crackenbury at opera, Mrs. Washington White in Ring). Instructs Smith to deny callers. Performs intense loyalty to King—name always on lips, proclaims him "most charming of men." Commissioned royal portrait from Colnaghi's (monarch in frock-coat with fur collar); wears portrait in brooch; pestered acquaintances with talk of his "urbanity and beauty." **Rumor**: May consider role of Maintenon or Pompadour.
- **Elaborate toilette preparation for Steyne visits (Chapter 21)**: Hair in perfect order, arranged artlessly. When surprised, rushes to apartment to survey self in glass and apply rouge before descending. Steyne caught her at this, heard her overhead, joked about giving rouge to Lady Gaunt whose "complexion is quite preposterous." Rebecca denied rouge, claimed genuine blushes and modesty. Narrator notes some rouge won't come off on handkerchief; some so good tears won't disturb it.
- **Dramatic confrontation with Steyne (Chapter 21)**: Steyne made lengthy speech comparing her to earthenware pipkin competing with copper kettles; complained of dining with King yesterday—"neck of mutton and turnips"; mocked Gaunt House as boring, wife "gay as Lady Macbeth," daughters "cheerful as Regan and Goneril"; sleeps in dressing-room on hair mattress "like an anchorite"; warned her to "hold your own" against female bullying at Gaunt House. Teased her about wanting Gaunt House invitation; she manipulated his irritation with Briggs by laughing mischievously, then feigned misery claiming "I could not help it. It was my only chance. I dare not tell my husband. He would kill me if I told him what I have done. I have kept it a secret from everybody but you--and you forced it from me." Steyne exited angrily beating "devil's tattoo" and biting nails. **Rebecca's true reaction**: Rose "with the queerest expression of victorious mischief glittering in her green eyes," burst laughing, sat at piano playing "triumphant voluntary."
- **Financial transactions with Steyne's assistance (Chapter 21)**: Received invitation to dinner at Gaunt House next Friday and slip of gray paper bearing Steyne's signature with address "Messrs. Jones, Brown, and Robinson, Lombard Street" (bank). **Bank visit**: In modest dress with veil, took hackney-coach to City, requested "hundred and fifty pounds in small notes and the remainder in one note." Paid Briggs handsome black silk gown. Gave Raggles fifty pounds on account. Gave livery-man Spavin fifty pounds, scolded him about carriage shortage forcing Colonel near-humiliation at prior drawing-room day (nearly forced to enter Royal presence in hack cab). Placed remainder note in Amelia's desk.
- **Steyne's family confrontation and Rebecca's ascendancy (Chapter 21 – NEW)**: Steyne declared to wife Lady Steyne: "You purchased a contingent reversion with it...If Gaunt dies, your husband may come to his honours; your little boys may inherit them...This Temple of Virtue belongs to me. And if I invite all Newgate or all Bedlam here, by ------ they shall be welcome." Commanded Lady Gaunt to write invitation; she and her mother-in-law drove in person with "bitter and humiliated hearts" to leave cards on Rebecca. Invitation caused Rebecca "so much pleasure."
- **Rebecca at Gaunt House dinner (Chapter 21 – NEW)**: Presented to Prince of Peterwaradin and Princess (nobleman tightly girthed with large military chest and red collar of Golden Fleece; long, solemn, white countenance). Greeted Lord Steyne with great courtesy. Ladies made stately curtsies; elder lady gave cold, lifeless hand. Rebecca performed reverence claiming Steyne was her father's earliest friend and patron; Lord Steyne had purchased couple of pictures from late Sharp. **Confrontation with Lady Bareacres**: Remarked upon previous acquaintance at Brussels ten years ago at Duchess of Richmond's ball (night before Battle of Waterloo), recalled seeing Lady Bareacres and Lady Blanche in carriage waiting for horses, inquired about her diamonds. Revealed famous diamonds had undergone "famous seizure" about which Becky professed ignorance. Rawdon laughed with Lord Southdown at story; Becky thought "I needn't be afraid of THAT woman." Lady Bareacres retreated terrified and angry. **French language superiority**: Spoke superior French accent when Danube Potentate arrived; had met Hungarian magnates with army in France 1816-17; foreign personages asked Lord Steyne and Marchioness who was "that petite dame who spoke so well?"
- **Female cruelty and Lady Steyne's compassion (Chapter 21 – NEW)**: Among ladies alone, experienced marked cruelty—great ladies avoided her, Master George Gaunt called away by his mamma, treated with such cruelty that even Lady Steyne pitied her. **Sang religious Mozart songs**: Performed songs that were early favorites of Lady Steyne with such sweetness and tenderness that lady sat by piano's side with tears rolling down her eyes, lost in childhood memories of convent garden and beloved chapel organist sister. Opposition ladies kept up loud buzzing in distance; Lady Steyne did not hear rumors, wandered "back through a forty years' wilderness to her convent garden." When men entered with Lord Steyne's loud laugh, he observed what occurred and expressed gratitude to his wife for once. Told Becky: "My wife says you have been singing like an angel...Now there are angels of two kinds, and both sorts, it is said, are charming in their way."
- **Contempt for Lady Jane**: Profound dissembler hiding scorn as "annoying."
- **Maternal rejection (unchanged)**: Would have preferred to leave little Rawdon behind.

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Baronet, MP**
- **Parliamentary ambition and dissembling**: Profound dissembler; attends assiduously, learns House routine thoroughly, makes acquaintance with ministers and party chiefs.
- **Emotional dependency on Rebecca intensifying**: Each day returns with "increasing gladness"; felt "quite a pang at departing" when leaving for Christmas.
- **Court presentation duty**: Drives to Curzon Street in new family carriage in "glittering uniform" with sword to convey Rebecca; acts as escort after presentation.
- **Secret gift to Rebecca**: Gave diamond clasp confined to pearl necklace; omitted mentioning to Lady Jane; blushed when mentioned.
- **Financial circumstances**: Knows brother's family has nothing; aware he appropriated money for younger brother; gave draft on bankers for hundred pounds before Christmas.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley**
- **Complete subjugation**: "Beat and cowed into laziness and submission." "Bold and reckless young blood of ten-years back was subjugated and was turned into a torpid, submissive, middle-aged, stout gentleman."
- **Deceived regarding jewels**: Knew nothing about brilliant diamonds. Rebecca lied claiming hired; Steyne knew truth.
- **Unaware of Steyne arrangement**: Heard Becky laughing in night; she claimed delight at going to Gaunt House; he unaware of her actual financial transactions and manipulations. At Gaunt House dinner, laughed with Lord Southdown at Lady Bareacres' degradation.
- **Strong attachment to little Rawdon**: Wraps boy in shawls; hoists onto coach roof; walks and rides with brother Pitt.

**Little Rawdon (Son)**
- **Character and activities**: Fine open-faced boy with blue eyes and waving flaxen hair; about eight years old; generous and soft in heart. At Christmas entered "perfect palace of enchantment and wonder" at Hall; experiences "extreme" happiness; wonderstruck by fox-hunt spectacle. Called away by his mamma at Gaunt House.

**Amelia Osborne (Mrs. George Osborne)**
- **Maternal integrity and sacrifice**: Refuses Mr. Osborne's formal offer conditioned on separation; tears letter into "hundred fragments"; calls proposal cowardly. Sacrifices personal purse to keep son in health despite financial ruin.
- **Conscience crisis**: Recognizes "her selfishness was sacrificing the boy" after mother's reproach; "tender and stricken heart" but does not alter refusal. Seeds of terrible doubt planted.
- **Old desk (unchanged)**: Years ago gave Rebecca a desk now containing Rebecca's diamonds and valuables hidden from Rawdon.

**The Marquis of Steyne and Gaunt Family**
- **Steyne's role in Rebecca's triumph (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Present at Court as Lord of the Powder Closet; "knew whence the jewels came and who paid for them"—**financed Rebecca's court diamonds**. Visits Rebecca regularly at Curzon Street; catches her preparing toilette with rouge; jokes intimately. Made bank arrangement with her (Messrs. Jones, Brown, and Robinson, Lombard Street) providing substantial sum. Sent invitation to Gaunt House dinner next Friday. At dinner, greeted Rebecca with great courtesy, presented her to Lady Steyne and daughters (whose curtsey was cold and lifeless). Observed Rebecca sing Mozart and moved Lady Steyne to tears; expressed gratitude to wife and complemented Rebecca ("like an angel"), with ambiguous suggestion of multiple types of angels.
- **Domestic tyranny (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Dominates household through bullying. When household discussed Rebecca, "battle royal ensued." Commanded respect by telling Lady Steyne she has "no money...no brains...were here to have children, and you have not had any. Gaunt's tired of you, and George's wife is the only person in the family who doesn't wish you were dead." Defended Rebecca: "My wife...has no objection to meet my young friend Mrs. Crawley." Asserted "appearances are sometimes against the best of women; that lies are often told about the most innocent of them." Threatened anecdotes about Lady Bareacres. To daughter Blanche cautioned against pride and self-airs. Compared Rebecca's ancestry favorably (noting first de la Jones ancestry less distinguished than Fanny's illustrious ancestor). **Forced obedience**: After vigorous allocution, "crestfallen women had nothing for it but to obey. Lady Gaunt wrote the invitation which his Lordship required." Declared himself master of Gaunt House: "This Temple of Virtue belongs to me. And if I invite all Newgate or all Bedlam here, by ------ they shall be welcome."
- **Haunting dread (unchanged)**: Tormented by ancestral curse affecting Lord George Gaunt.
- **Lord George Gaunt's institutionalization (unchanged)**: Institutionalized for mental illness after breakdown; mother visits twice or thrice weekly.
- **Lady Steyne characterization (Chapter 21 – NEW)**: Held "very highest rank in Vanity Fair"; severe, spotless, and beautiful. Had convent childhood with beloved organist sister; experienced early happiness in chapel; religious devotion preserved. Moved to tears by Rebecca's Mozart singing; revealed tender memory of childhood refuge and lost happiness.
- **Contingent reversion (Chapter 21 – NEW)**: Steyne revealed to wife that Rebecca and Rawdon "purchased a contingent reversion"—if Gaunt dies, Rawdon may come to honours; little boys may inherit them.

**Old Mr. Sedley**
- **Financial decline**: Dabbles in speculation despite Clapp's remonstrances; wine and coal companies failed; bills in arrear.

**Mrs. Sedley**
- **Anguished desperation**: Growing infirm; weeps frequently; made hysterical outburst accusing Amelia.

**Mrs. Bute Crawley**
- **Resentful reaction**: Read newspaper account of Becky's Court presentation with "bitterness of spirit"; consulted Morning Post with daughters in country; vented "honest indignation" at Becky's "airs."

## Critical Facts (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)
- **Steyne finances Rebecca's diamonds and provides banking arrangement**: Diamond ear-rings never returned to Polonius; hidden in Amelia's desk. Steyne paid for them. Provided bank access (Messrs. Jones, Brown, and Robinson) from which Rebecca withdrew substantial funds (at least 250 pounds distributed). **Implicit sexual/financial arrangement** suspected between Steyne and Rebecca.
- **Rebecca's manipulative mastery**: Feigned victimhood with Steyne (encouraging his annoyance), then expressed "victorious mischief" after departure. At Gaunt House, revealed prior knowledge of Lady Bareacres' diamond seizure, intimidated her into silence, established French linguistic superiority, sang Mozart moving Lady Steyne emotionally while enduring female cruelty.
- **Rebecca's calculated benevolence**: Distributed money to Briggs, Raggles, and livery-man Spavin strategically.
- **Steyne's despotic authority**: Dominates household through threats, contempt, and force of will. Defends Rebecca publicly to family members, forcing their obedience and acceptance. Declared Gaunt House his personal property with absolute dominion over guests invited.
- **Rebecca's calculated ascendancy at Gaunt House**: Dinner invitation and bank arrangement indicate planned financial and social triumph. Steyne's public support ensures her acceptance despite female jealousy and cruelty. Reference to "contingent reversion" suggests Steyne's investment in Rawdon's potential future title/fortune through Rebecca.
